title: Luminate Adds Songwriter and Publishing Information to Service
summary: Available for an additional fee, Luminate now allows users to dig into songwriter and publisher information, thanks to new partnerships with CISAC and the MLC.
contentText:
Entertainment data platform Luminate has added music publishing and songwriter data to its CONNECT service, starting Wednesday (Nov. 18). Available for an additional fee, Luminate users can now see the information and activity attached to musical works as well as recordings on the platform for the first time.

The data is sourced from Luminate’s partnerships with CISAC and the MLC along with “proprietary data and advanced matching logic,” as a blog post about the news states. Use cases for this publishing data — which provides information about the songwriters and underlying song copyright — include the ability to audit and evaluate which recordings are driving the most sales and streams for a given song and the ability to see and export tables of ISWC (the unique code given to every registered musical work/song) and ISRC (the unique code given to every registered sound recording) links quickly.

Over time, Luminate plans to track publishing rights to musical works and display which songwriters and publishers control those rights on their dashboards.

According to the blog post, written by Luminate’s chief product officer Arnaud Retureau , there are several expected benefits of its new publishing data: music publishers can “see how every version of a work is performing worldwide,” investors can “get a clearer foundation for forecasting a catalog’s value over time,” performing rights organizations (PROs) can better “monitor their registered ISWCs for future royalty payments,” labels and distributors can “clean up metadata” and “check release readiness” and streaming services can get a clearer view of publishing rights.

Nearly 150,000 Tracks Are Added to Streaming Services Every Day, Luminate CEO Says

Providing transparency about publishing data has long been a challenge in the music business. Often, songs — also called “musical works” — are written by several songwriters, all of whom are represented by music publishers. Given the song is owned by a complex web of rights holders, it’s much more common to find clerical errors in publishing registrations than it is on the recorded music side. To make the system even worse, sometimes recordings are released on streaming services without the songwriters finalizing the arrangement of who owns what part of the publishing, leading to even more issues within the system.

The news comes just months after Luminate announced its plans to add labels to AI music on its service. Set to launch later this year, the company aims to identify these AI works with a combination of its own identification system, data from streaming services and information from the AI music companies themselves.
